\opt{C}{Ratio of potential at centre of disc to potential at centre of solid sphere is $\dfrac{2}{\pi}$}
\opt{D}{Ratio of potential at centre of disc to potential at centre of solid sphere is $\dfrac{4}{3}$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SA22-P2-PHY-S3-G17-18, source={Score Advanced - Test 22 (10 Apr 2024)}, questions={17-18}]
Consider first a metal sphere of radius R and total charge Q, which (because of symmetry) is distributed uniformly on its surface, i.e. the surface charge density is $\sigma_0=\dfrac{Q}{4\pi R^2}$ = constant.\par
The total field effects of the charges on the small surface pieces opposite each other cancel out in pairs, so the net electric field of all the charges on the sphere is zero at any point P inside the sphere. The same is shown in figure-1.\par
\bfig{92.7}{SA22_p2_phy_s3_para17_18_1.png}
\bfig{93.4}{SA22_p2_phy_s3_para17_18_2.png}
Now let us move on to the case of the electrically charged metal disc. We show that its charge distribution can be found from the uniform surface density of the charged metal sphere. Let us (notionally) `glue into position' the charges on the surface of the sphere, and then project the points of the spherical surface perpendicularly onto a plane that contains the centre of the sphere and point P investigated earlier.\par
As the charges cannot move, the charge $\Delta Q_1$, originally on the surface area $\Delta A_1$, when projected onto the plane, occupies a somewhat smaller area $\Delta A_1^{*}$, and so the surface charge density (with an unchanged amount of charge) increases. In addition, its distance from the point P also changes, from the original value of $r_1$ to the smaller one of $d_1$. The corresponding thing happens with the charge $\Delta Q_2$ originally located on the opposite side of the sphere.
\end{bankpassage}

An electric dipole has a fixed dipole moment $\vec p$, which makes angle $\theta$ with respect to $x$-axis. When subjected to an electric field $\vec E_1=E\hat i$, it experiences a torque $\vec T_1=\tau\hat k$. When subjected to another electric field $\vec E_2=\sqrt3E_1\hat j$ it experiences torque $\vec T_2=-\vec T_1$. The angle $\theta$ is :
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$60^\circ$}
\opt{B}{$90^\circ$}
\opt{C}{$30^\circ$}
\opt{D}{$45^\circ$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=TNAS03-P2-PHY-S1-Q03, source={TNAS - Test 03 (28 May 2023)}, paper=2, qno=3, type=multi, subtopic={Electric potential}, answer={A,C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K1 S2 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: charge crossing a potential step | steps: energy condition; angle of motion; fraction crossing}]
A positively charged particle is accelerated from the origin with the help of a voltage $4U$ (where $U>0$) to a certain velocity which lies on the $x-y$ plane under the angle of 30 degrees with respect to the $x$-axis (see figure). The electric potential $V(x,y)=V(x)$ only depends on the $x$-coordinate: if $3a<x<4a$ then $V\{x\}=U$ and if not then $V(x)=0$; besides the electrostatic force no other forces are applied to the particle and $a>0$.\\
For option C \& D consider the source of the charged particles is now a coaxial vacuum diode at the origin. Because of that the particles accelerated with the voltage $4U$ are moving isotropically (at equal quantities) to all directions of the $x-y$ plane; the $z$-directional component of the velocity for all particles is 0.
\bfig{92.5}{TNAS03_p2_phy_s1_q03_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The trajectory of the charge on x-y plane will be \bfigi{31.8}{TNAS03_p2_phy_s1_q03_2.png}.}
\opt{B}{The trajectory of the charge on x-y plane will be \bfigi{36.2}{TNAS03_p2_phy_s1_q03_3.png}.}
\opt{C}{The part of all the emitted particles that reaches the region of space $x>4a$ is $\dfrac13$.}
\opt{D}{The part of all the emitted particles that reaches the region of space $x>4a$ is $\dfrac23$.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
